companies.name: Mission d’Appui à la Conduite d’Opérations Municipales (MACOM)
companies.role: Chosen as the project’s implementing and coordinating agency because its procurement and accounting staff already knew Bank procedures; the project coordination unit under it recruited a safeguards expert and a social expert in January 2009, who worked with the Agence Nationale de l’Environnement. The completion report names no construction contractor.

community: Resettlement plans were prepared for four sites in Abidjan: the footbridge at Williamsville, the underpass at Riviera 2, the road at M’Badon, and the bridge and connecting road over the ravine in Cocody. The borrower’s report, printed as an annex to the completion report, says unforeseen impacts on local residents occurred during the rehabilitation of the M’Badon road, where access to shops was restricted, and during the construction of the Cocody zone 7-9 bridge, where third parties were damaged when a site access road was opened. For those cases it says the coordination unit “has ensured that Project-Affected Persons (PAPs) were duly compensated”, and that “a total of 629 PAPs have been compensated to the amount of FCFA 857,568,478 for a total of 639 PAPs identified. It remains to reimburse the salaries of 10 store employees affected by the Riviera 2 constructions due to technical unemployment, for whom salaries were pre-financed by employers, who have however failed to produce documentary evidence of this pre-financing to justify their refund.” On the annex’s account the ten were paid their wages by their employers; what remained unpaid was the project’s reimbursement of those wages. The completion report rates the overall project outcome Satisfactory (paragraph 46). No Independent Evaluation Group review of this report was reachable.

lenders.role: Facility Agent for the lenders; the completion report says it led supervision of plant construction and of compliance with the Bank’s environmental and social safeguards, through an independent owner’s engineer

companies.role: Independent power producer created in 2008 to build and run the plant; the project’s implementing agency and borrower under the guaranteed loans

companies.name: Wartsila
companies.role: Named in the completion report as the only bidder to propose a detailed binding offer for the larger plant and as offering the lowest cost of generated electricity; the report says the choice of gas engines for the plant was made on the basis of that offer. It does not record who supplied the engines.

companies.name: Siemens France
companies.role: With KEC India, the preferred bidder for the engineering, procurement and construction contract on the 225 kV transmission line and the 11/225 kV substation

companies.name: KEC India
companies.role: Consortium partner with Siemens France on the transmission line and substation contract, as named in the completion report

companies.name: Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH)
companies.role: Cameroon’s state hydrocarbons company and sponsor of the Sanaga South gas pipeline that fuels the plant; through its Comité de Pilotage et de Suivi des Pipelines it assessed and paid the compensation for the Bipaga access road

community: The completion report says the 2012 annual monitoring report recorded the physical resettlement of 23 families, compensation for crops destroyed outside the transmission line corridor, and the restoration of polluted water courses. The completion report puts the onshore gas pipeline inside the project as an associated facility, within the scope of the environmental and social impact assessment updated in 2010. For the access road from the Edéa–Kribi national road to the SNH site at Bipaga, built for SNH’s own Sanaga-Sud pipeline project, a compensation note disclosed under the Bank project in March 2012 records payments actually made: 24 people were compensated for crops in the right of way, on the basis of expert valuation sheets listing the crops, the number of plants and the amount; three private properties with land titles were partly taken, of 5,543 square metres (FCFA 27,715,000), 846 square metres (FCFA 8,460,000) and 1,360 square metres (FCFA 6,800,000); and houses lost were paid for at market economic value, with the buildings described as mostly built of temporary materials. The payments were made on 23 September 2010 and 3 December 2010, a year before the Bank’s Board approved the guarantee, out of SNH’s own budget under Prime Ministerial Decree 2010/2341/PM of 3 August 2010, some by cheque and some in cash. SNH says the payments were peaceful and on time and that no dispute was recorded, and that the people living around the access road carried on farming, fishing and working in Kribi. Once the plant was running, low-frequency noise from the engines disturbed the villages around it. Measured noise was slightly above World Health Organization and IFC levels, but so were the baseline levels taken before the plant ran, which the report puts down to the site and the nearby highways. Local communities complained of vibration in their homes. KPDC insulated the roofs of affected homes with noise-suppression material and built a noise barrier wall near the turbines. The project also had an Indigenous Peoples Plan covering Bakola communities along the transmission line; on this the completion report records only that KPDC worked with the NGO Cameroon Ecology to help carry the plan out, and gives no outcome for those communities.
outcome: The 216 MW plant was built and the completion report rates the project Satisfactory. The report also records that electricity supply from KPDC depends on the government paying a tariff compensation to the distributor ENEO to cover the gap between its costs and regulated tariffs, and that payments were irregular.

title: Compensation still unpaid months after closing in Cameroon’s urban upgrading project
place: Yaoundé, with works also in Douala, Bamenda, Maroua and Mbalmayo, Cameroon

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban and Water Development Support Project, known as PDUE (P084002), IDA credit 4313-CM of SDR 53.3 million (US$80 million equivalent) and an additional financing, credit 4820-CM, of SDR 18.9 million (US$28.7 million equivalent) from Pilot Crisis Response Window resources; Board approval 29 May 2007, actual closing 31 August 2015 (completion report ICR00003619, 29 February 2016; evaluation review ICRR0020199, 28 June 2016). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Both documents rate the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the risk to development outcome High.

companies.name: Project Coordination Unit, Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (MINHDU)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the urban components, a unit kept inside MINHDU after closing; it paid compensation directly or through the municipalities. The completion report names no construction contractor.

community: The completion report says counterpart money was secured so that the project unit, directly or through the municipalities, could pay compensation to the 585 people affected by the project. Of those, 88 per cent had been compensated as of 31 January 2016, against 51 per cent at the closing date of 31 August 2015, for CFAF 401 million, which the report puts at 88 per cent of the amount due. The report says payments had markedly progressed since the closing date “but two for Yaoundé were still awaiting the presidential clearance at the time of this report”. The Bank’s involuntary resettlement policy was rated only partly complied with, Moderately Unsatisfactory in early 2014 and again at closing. The report says the delays were beyond the project’s control: the national rules for taking land and paying for it ran through several administrative steps, including a Presidential Decree clearing the list of affected people that could take months to come out, and further decrees were needed to add people left out of the first assessments. Phase 2 resettlement plans were approved only at the end of 2014. For Phase 1 the report says no standalone resettlement plans had been prepared where works cut across parts of urban plots, while adding that “in practice though, as noted in supervision reports, the PCU had complied with the policy’s requirements through consultations on the project’ benefits”. It says that in many cases owners agreed to hand land over to the public domain with no money paid, which saved time on the works, and that other families were paid for damage. For Phase 2 the rule was tightened so that works could not start before people were paid. The report says full payment of the outstanding compensation “remains of utmost importance”, and that the Bank made fully resolving the compensation legacy a condition of approving a follow-on operation.
outcome: Payments had moved on since the closing date but were not finished when the completion report was written in February 2016, with two for Yaoundé awaiting presidential clearance. The Bank attached the condition that the compensation legacy be fully resolved before the follow-on “Inclusive Cities” operation went to its Board.

title: Resettled people inadequately compensated on the Congo road works, with 61 per cent of the National Road 2 payments made at closing
place: National Road 6 from Akula to Gemena, Mbari, Libenge and Zongo, Équateur, and National Road 5 from Lubumbashi to Kasomeno and Kasenga, Katanga, Democratic Republic of the Congo

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P088619, Emergency Living Conditions Improvement Support Project (ELCISP). IDA Grant H1640, SDR 53.90 million, of which SDR 53.87 million was disbursed. Approved 26 May 2005, original closing 30 September 2010, actual closing 30 June 2012 after three restructurings, the last on 22 February 2012 (completion report ICR2521, 21 December 2012). Environmental category B. Five safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome High, and Bank and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review of 23 September 2013 rates implementing agency performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and overall borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and says that on the information given it cannot be concluded that there was compliance with the environmental safeguard policies.

companies.name: Unité de Coordination de Projets (UCoP), Democratic Republic of the Congo
companies.role: The government project coordination unit that implemented the project. The completion report says a lack of oversight by it led to the corruption case the Bank's integrity unit investigated, and the borrower's own report names inadequate monitoring of environmental and social aspects during construction among the weaknesses a technical audit found.

companies.name: Bureau Central de Coordination (BCECO), Democratic Republic of the Congo
companies.role: One of the delegated contract managers for the works; it was trained by an international environmental and social consulting firm hired after the mid-term review.

community: The grant rehabilitated National Road 6 from Akula through Gemena and Mbari to Libenge and Zongo in Équateur and National Road 5 from Lubumbashi through Kasomeno to Kasenga in Katanga, and funded urban works in several towns. The completion report says the mid-term review "revealed that project affected persons resettled due to the road construction were not adequately compensated, that the works contracts did not, as foreseen, include funding to mitigate environmental aspects, and that the problem of medical wastes from health facilities funded by the project was not fully taken into account". An international environmental and social consulting firm was then hired to train the project unit, the contractors and the delegated contract manager, and management plans were drawn up for each 30-kilometre road segment. A total of 627 project-affected persons were compensated. At project closing the beneficiary satisfaction survey found no adequate solution to the medical waste. The report also covers National Road 2, rehabilitated under an earlier Bank-financed project: no displacement or asset losses occurred there, but the road shoulders were cut back, leaving almost no space between the road and neighbouring buildings and raising the risk of traffic accidents. An after-the-fact resettlement plan was prepared for that road and was to be paid for by this project, but a change in the lender's rules stopped cash compensation being paid from its funds. The government has implemented the plan as money became available and had paid 61 per cent of the amount due to 35 project-affected persons. The amount is given as US$262,090 in the completion report and as US$202,090 in the Evaluation Group's review. The Group's review adds that an indigenous peoples plan was prepared and circulated to non-governmental organisations, academics, Pygmy associations and news agencies, and that no information is given on whether it was carried out.
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2012. At that point 61 per cent of the National Road 2 compensation had been paid to 35 people and the rest was being paid by the government as funds allowed; the medical waste problem was unsolved. The completion report also records a corruption case investigated by the lender's integrity unit, and an advance of US$1.4 million on a road contract cancelled in 2010 for non-performance that had still not been repaid when the report was written.

title: Works started before resettlement, a worker badly injured, and a complainant threatened in Mbandaka
place: Mbandaka, with works also in Bukavu, Goma, Kalemie, Kananga, Kikwit, Kindu, Kisangani, Kolwezi and Matadi, Democratic Republic of Congo

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban Development Project (P129713), IDA grant H8420-ZR of SDR 66.1 million (US$100 million equivalent) and credit 6034-ZR of SDR 66.5 million (US$90 million equivalent), the completion report’s cover giving them as IDA-H8420 and IDA-60340; Board approval 9 May 2013, actual closing 30 July 2021; total project cost US$108,159,215 against an appraisal estimate of US$190,000,000 (completion report ICR00005701, 17 February 2022; evaluation review ICRR0022973, 31 August 2022). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. The completion report rates the overall outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory (paragraph 47); the Independent Evaluation Group also rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory. The geographic scope went from six cities to nine with the additional financing and was then cut to four — Bukavu, Goma, Kikwit and Matadi — in the 2020 restructuring, with Kananga added afterwards.

companies.name: Secrétariat Permanent, Projet de Développement Urbain, Ministère de l’Urbanisme et Habitat
companies.role: The project’s permanent secretariat inside the Congolese Ministry of Urban Planning and Housing, through its Cellule Environnementale et Sociale; it prepared the quarterly safeguards reports, ran the censuses and reported on the resettlement payments

companies.name: China First
companies.role: Named in the project’s February 2019 mission report as the contractor on the Avenue Gazumbu works in Kolwezi, where the mission was also to check that the firm’s environmental officer and sociologist had been put on site and to visit its camp and borrow pits

community: The completion report counts 1,078 people affected by the project, identified through resettlement plans, of whom 1,041 were compensated for a total of US$155,918. The report says the rest did not present themselves to receive compensation, that the secretariat and local authorities tried to locate and contact them in each case, and that US$18,984 has been reserved with the local governments should those efforts succeed; it does not print a figure for how many people that is. Seventy-nine occupational health and safety incidents were recorded. Seventy-five were minor, three were serious and one, a fall from height causing serious injury, was treated as severe and reported to Bank management through its incident response procedure; the report says root causes were analysed, corrective measures developed, and the secretariat supplied documentation of the injured person’s treatment and full recovery. Three cases of non-compliance were documented. Two were works starting before the resettlement plan had been carried out, one of them before the contract had even been signed; in one of those the Bank told the government the investment would not be eligible for project money and no project funds were used, which a footnote gives as the reason no infrastructure was financed by the project in Goma, and in the other the resettlement plan was updated and the works allowed to continue. In Kolwezi, a project mission in February 2019 found 13 people losing income on Avenue Gazumbu — among them a hairdresser, a phone-kiosk operator and a pharmacy seller, listed by name, with GPS points, and assessed at US$1,195 in all, of which US$150 was assistance to people counted as vulnerable — whom an earlier consultant had missed: the 2016 study reported finding no affected people on that avenue, so no resettlement plan was written, no cut-off date was published and no signs were put up to stop new occupation of the right of way. The mayor’s office said it was ready to pay the 13 so they would clear the route before works began. At Kananga, the project’s own report on carrying out the resettlement plan for the erosion-control works at the MONUSCO site records that on 16 June 2021 one household head, counted as 15 affected persons, was paid US$5,650, all of what the plan provided: US$4,000 for the house and US$1,600 for fruit trees and family crops, with US$50 for one person assessed as vulnerable. Kananga city hall put up US$4,000 of that and the project US$1,650, in a table the report heads as funds for paying affected people who had been left out. The report says the household, that of Laurent Nkashama, moved into a house bought on the spot before the old one was pulled down, that the operation passed without incident, and that a grievance committee opened its registers at the town hall and in Mulombodi quarter on 19 June 2021.
outcome: All the safety cases and the grievances were recorded as closed before the project ended. US$18,984 of compensation stayed unpaid, reserved with local governments for the affected people who never came forward. The completion report rates the project Moderately Unsatisfactory overall, and says Kananga still faces serious gully erosion threatening other infrastructure.

place: Mont Kimwenza Sebo, Kimbondo and the Lukaya river, Mont Ngafula, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo

lenders.role: Emergency Urban and Social Rehabilitation Project, known as PURUS (P104497), IDA grant H282-ZR of SDR 120 million (US$180 million equivalent) and an additional grant H596-ZR of SDR 26.5 million (US$40 million equivalent) from the Crisis Response Window; Board approval 29 March 2007, closing 31 May 2013 against an original date of 31 May 2011 (completion report ICR00002732, 27 November 2013; evaluation review ICRR14385, 29 July 2014). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Both documents rate the overall outcome Satisfactory. community: The water component extended the distribution network into poor quarters in the south and south-west of Kinshasa, in the communes of Mont Ngafula, Ngaliema, Lemba and Selembao, and built two reservoirs on the Mont Kimwenza Sebo and Kimbondo hills, a pumping station, and a catchment plant on the Lukaya river. It records the destruction across the three hill sites of various buildings, small houses, fences and foundations, and at the Lukaya site 72 fruit trees and 3 food gardens of cassava, and a permanent loss of 9,306 square metres of cultivable land, which it gives as 517 market-garden beds. outcome: The compensation was paid and the works went ahead from January 2011. The completion report records no unpaid balance and no dispute over the payments.

title: Twenty-Three Land Parcels and Eighty-Four Easements Were Still Unsettled When Colombia's Water Loan Closed
place: Water and sanitation sub-projects in municipalities across Colombia, with two families awaiting resettlement in the municipality of Neiva, Huila

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Water and Sanitation Sector Support Project, first phase of an adaptable programme loan (P082973), Loan 7281-CO, seventy million dollars, loan agreement with the Republic of Colombia dated 2 June 2005. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says the project was Category B and, "according to the POAD, triggered four safeguards policies: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Cultural Property (OP 4.11), Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12), and Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10)". The three Bank documents disagree on the outcome and each rating is taken from the document that gave it: the completion report of 30 March 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the evaluation review's ratings table gives Moderately Satisfactory for both the report and the evaluation group, with no disagreement recorded; the Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, a joint assessment of three Colombian water projects, rates this project's overall outcome moderately unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome substantial. The review says an important cause of delay was "the difficulty in obtaining right of way permits (for easements), acquire land, and implement resettlement in accordance with social safeguards", and that sub-projects expected to take 16 months took 44 on average, the project closing 23 months late.

companies.name: Ministerio de Ambiente, Vivienda y Desarrollo Territorial
companies.role: The Colombian environment, housing and territorial development ministry, which ran the project through its vice-ministry for water and sanitation, hired three extra social specialists to work with the sub-projects and to draw up and supervise the remedial action plans, and was overseeing the unresolved parcels and easements directly at closing. In its comments on the completion report the ministry said the involuntary resettlement policy framework prepared for the project was unclear, and that completing the requirements in the remaining sub-projects "had a high cost for the nation".

companies.name: Fondo Financiero de Proyectos de Desarrollo (FONADE)
companies.role: The Colombian state development project financing agency, which administered the sub-projects. The evaluation review says provisions were made by FONADE for compliance with the safeguard policies, and that its capacity was weaker than the ministry's.

community:
This loan paid for water and sewerage works in municipalities across Colombia, chosen through an application window that 550 municipalities applied to. Getting the land and the rights of way for the pipes was the problem the project did not plan for. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says land acquisition and easement issues "are commonly encountered in water supply and sanitation projects. However, they were not adequately factored into project design."

The mid-term review found what the completion report of 30 March 2012 calls "substantive and procedural issues in the application of involuntary resettlement and indigenous peoples policies". The ministry hired three social specialists to carry out field evaluations and to design a remedial action plan for each sub-project that needed one. An overall social remediation plan was approved on 28 April 2010, five years into a project that closed in March 2011.

The completion report gives the position at closing. A Bank review showed the ministry had completed 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements satisfactorily. The remainder was unfinished: "The SRAP, however, is not complete as the resettlement of two families in the Municipality of Neiva and the legalization of 23 parcels and 84 easements are currently in progress." The report adds that full conformity was not realistic in the short term because most of the parcel and easement cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures, and that the Bank would keep supervising the borrower's progress. The evaluation review puts the same facts as compensation: "At project closure in March 2011, compensation issues related to the legalization of 23 land parcels and 84 easements were still unresolved."

The ministry's own comments in the completion report say the involuntary resettlement policy framework prepared for the project was unclear, and that although it was committed to completing the requirements in the remaining sub-projects, doing so "had a high cost for the nation".
outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2011, having been due to close on 30 April 2009. At closing 23 parcels and 84 easements were unsettled and two families in Neiva were still to be resettled, and the completion report says most of those cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, five years later, repeats the figures of 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements completed satisfactorily and does not say what became of the rest, the two families in Neiva or the unsettled cases. It rates this project's outcome moderately unsatisfactory, against the moderately satisfactory of the completion report and of the evaluation review.

The project was later run under a Temporary Administration (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 15 October 2018).

companies.name: Aguas de La Guajira S.A. E.S.P.
companies.role: The operator of the water supply system. The indigenous resettlement plan records that one of the two stated grounds for the temporary suspension of works contract No. 487 of 2001, on 22 December 2006, was that this operator had not met its commitment to supply water or to make the missing connections to the pipes already laid, which was one of the undertakings agreed with the community in the consultation meetings (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

companies.name: Fundación MANA
companies.role: The foundation that prepared the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan for the Riohacha wastewater system under Convenio 013 de 2009 with the department (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

community:
The project built water and sanitation works across La Guajira, a department whose rural population is largely Wayuu. Nine Wayuu communities stood in the direct area of influence of the wastewater treatment lagoons planned for Riohacha: 110 families and 518 people, by the census in the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan of June 2011. El Arroyo, La Loma and Campo Alegre were the largest.

Consultation on the lagoons ran for years. The plan records that works contract No. 487 of 2001 was suspended again on 22 December 2006 on two stated grounds: that the water operator had not met its commitment to supply water or complete the missing pipe connections, one of the undertakings agreed with the community, and that the indigenous families settled in the direct area of influence now had to be relocated. In December 2008 two meetings fixed commitments on housing and land purchase and the governor signed an undertaking for the definitive move of the families from the direct area. A list of commitments agreed between 2008 and 2010 includes school classrooms, a school canteen and sanitary units at La Loma, aqueduct pipes for La Loma and Guayabito on relocation, a reservoir, sixteen water tanks across sixteen communities, electricity networks for the relocated sections, a housing subsidy for seven families at Cuatro Bocas, and payment for improvements plus a housing improvement subsidy of up to 5,000,000 pesos each at 2,200,000 pesos a hectare for the land ceded.

The completion report of 15 October 2018 says the indigenous resettlement plan was 96 per cent complete at the time of the report and that the one outstanding commitment for the resettled houses was electrification, for which the government had budgeted but which the project did not deliver. It records that although the project "developed safeguards instruments and carried out consultations in compliance with the policies", it "met significant resistance given that: (i) the municipalities/departments were not complying with the agreements established in the consultations; and (ii) with each consultation, the Project received more demands". The same table records the indigenous peoples plan for the reservoirs as complete and the one for Maicao as 95 per cent complete.

The Riohacha lagoon construction contract was signed in January 2016 and suspended in July 2016 at 9 per cent physical progress, first because of community opposition and then because a new national rule required an archaeological plan, which was approved only at the project's closure. In Maicao the lagoon "was stalled because of complications around the purchase of land for the community members who had to relocate due to the construction of the lagoon. The lagoon was 95% complete when the communities started stalling the works because they had not received any of the benefits agreed on through 'Consulta Previa'/IPP at that time." The land was bought in November 2017 and construction had still not resumed when the report was written. The Maicao lagoons were not financed by the project, which the report says limited the Bank's leverage over safeguard compliance; the project supported the social component there through the indigenous peoples plan.

The department's rural reservoir programme, ten reservoirs in Uribia, was conceived outside the project and brought into it in 2011; the report says it "was not in compliance with Bank safeguards" and that the Bank's team asked for construction to be suspended for want of technical support, and that by the end of the project all the reservoirs were operational and in compliance. The project gave 8,881 Wayuu people improved water sources against a target of 3,500, built ten reservoirs against a target of eight, and cut the time spent fetching water by more than four hours; nine of the ten reservoirs held water fit to drink, and in the tenth, Gran Vía, it did not. Rural sanitation reached 468 Wayuu residents in Riohacha and 112 in Maicao.
outcome: The loan closed on 16 April 2018, six and a half years after the original closing date, with US$71.4 million of US$90 million disbursed. The Riohacha lagoons were 9 per cent built and the contract suspended; the Maicao lagoon was 95 per cent built and stalled. Electrification of the houses the resettled Wayuu families had been given was still outstanding, with the money budgeted by the Temporary Water Administration or the authority in charge. The micro-aqueduct meant to improve water supply to indigenous communities under the Maicao plan stood at 80 per cent. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Unsatisfactory.

title: Resettlement for the Ambouli dike at Djibouti city
place: Ambouli wadi and the PK 12 resettlement site, Djibouti city, Djibouti

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Flood Emergency Rehabilitation Project (P089968). Credit 3977-DJ and Grant H123-DJ, SDR 2.2 million credit and SDR 3.6 million grant, approved by the Board on 2 September 2004; the financing agreement and the project agreement were signed on 2 October 2004. Additional financing of SDR 1.4 million approved by the Board in February 2007 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 October 2009). The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 May 2010 rates it Moderately Unsatisfactory. Both rate the risk to the development outcome Significant. The completion report rates Bank performance Satisfactory; the review rates it Moderately Satisfactory. Both rate borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Agence Djiboutienne d'Execution des Travaux d'Interet Public (ADETIP)
companies.role: Government contract-management agency that ran the works and the resettlement site. In 2007 Parliament widened its mandate to the National Initiative for Human Development and it was renamed Agence Djiboutienne de Developpement Social (ADDS), into which ADETIP was folded. It did not report the jobs its labour-intensive works were meant to create.

companies.name: Housing Fund of the Ministry of Urban Development, Djibouti
companies.role: State fund that built the 277 dwellings at PK 12, called Cite Gargaar, and sold them to the resettled families on hire-purchase terms. It also produced the report on the resettled families' situation after the study the project had planned was dropped.

community: Floods on 13 April 2004 killed an estimated 100 people in Djibouti city and affected more than 100,000. The project rebuilt the Ambouli embankment dike and paid for basic services at a resettlement site 12 km out of the city, called PK 12. The completion report's indicator table says 100 per cent of families were resettled, and that this takes in "approx. 240 families affected by the flood and 120 affected by the dike construction and resettled later on". The report's account of the Bank's internal quality review puts it the same way: compensation for "some 120 families living on the reconstruction site, as well as another 240 families who were victims of the flood" had to be settled before the dike could be designed and tendered. The government's own completion report, printed inside the same document, gives different figures. It says the rehousing plan "involves 127 households, of whom 55 are victims of the flooding and 72 have been displaced by the dike reconstruction work". The Bank's text also says that out of 127 families eligible for resettlement at PK 12, 94 took a new house, 2 took a plot and the rest moved elsewhere. In the project's first year the government did not hand occupancy permits to the families moved to PK 12, did not provide their precise numbers or names, and postponed dealing with compensation; the permits were a condition of the credit for delivering latrines and water at the site. The resettlement plan the government filed in July 2006 does carry a named list, of 127 households living in 105 structures affected by the dike construction, with a cut-off date of 2 June 2005. The Bank's team recorded that the government was reluctant to apply the resettlement policy, which it considered too generous towards illegal squatters. At PK 12 the report says the new houses are better than those the flood destroyed and that water standpipes and latrines were provided, but that the families "have difficulty finding jobs, as the resettlement site is far from downtown Djibouti", and that several of the resettled families had made a living from vegetable gardening in the Ambouli river bed. At the last supervision meeting the residents said water supply had failed for the previous two months and that schools and work were far away. The report answers that the distance to the city centre is real but that no land was available for resettlement closer in. It says the resettlement action plan was in the end prepared and implemented in a satisfactory manner, and the evaluation review says all 360 families were given occupancy permits.
outcome: The dike was finished in March 2009, after the closing date had been pushed back from 30 September 2008. The completion report says some works to ease the flow of water in the river were still unfinished, partly because people had moved into the area, and that the government had not stopped people settling in the river bed and banks or dumping trash there. Financing was secured for an upstream dam at Boulle to take pressure off the dike. Of the 400 latrines planned for PK 12, 300 were built; the report says that number is sufficient for the resettled population.

title: Farmland and Cocoa Trees Taken Before Payment on Two Dominican Irrigation Works
place: The Canal Lateral Neyba between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, Neyba and Duvergé, Bahoruco and Independencia provinces; the La Gina irrigation system with the Arroyo Rico and Río Jayán dikes, Miches, El Seibo province; and the Yuna-Cañabón system, Bonao, Monseñor Nouel province, Dominican Republic

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Emergency Recovery and Disaster Management Project (P109932), Loan 7546-DO, eighty million dollars, agreement dated 27 May 2008 between the Dominican Republic and the IBRD. The completion report of 22 April 2017 says the project was rated Category B and that "Two policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37)"; it adds that the project did not expect to trigger either social safeguard policy and that only focal points for social safeguards were named in the implementing agencies. The evaluation review of 14 September 2017 gives the final list as Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The Involuntary Resettlement policy was added at a level one restructuring, which the completion report dates to November 2010 and which both the review and the completion report's own restructuring table date to 1 October 2010. That restructuring covered only the activities of CDEEE, the state electricity corporation, which is the project's other implementing agency; it did not create a resettlement instrument for the irrigation works carried out by INDRHI. The evaluation review dates the approval of an additional financing of twenty million dollars, Loan 8098, to 17 November 2011; the completion report says its loan agreement was signed on 18 November 2011, that the loan was terminated when the effectiveness deadline of 17 August 2012 was missed, and that it was reinstated with the deadline extended to 16 November 2012. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and so does the evaluation review; the review rates efficiency modest and efficacy substantial. The report says that in April 2014 it "appeared that INDRHI, which had limited knowledge of Bank Social Safeguards procedures, had begun expropriating farmers/private land owners in two locations in order to construct new canals/re-route existing canals", that "This situation occurred without the knowledge of the Bank and without the benefit of a project-level Resettlement Policy Framework in place", and that a Bank social specialist later "concluded that all persons who had been expropriated had received proper compensation". It says Resettlement Action Plans and Remedial Action Plans were prepared "although with important delays", were acceptable to the Bank, and that by closing the project was in compliance with OP 4.12. In its section on Bank performance the report says the Bank team "may have anticipated and prevented irregularities that occurred within INDRHI's activities" if the policy had been triggered project-wide in 2010, and that the team "took rapid action when INDRHI was found to be in non-compliance regarding the displacement of people, an element not covered at that time by a Bank pre-approved Resettlement Plan".

companies.name: Instituto Nacional de Recursos Hidráulicos (INDRHI)
companies.role: The Dominican state's water resources institute, which built and rehabilitated the irrigation systems and carried out the expropriations. Its Departamento de Derecho de Vía, the right-of-way department, valued the plots and trees and signed the agreements with owners, working with the project's own execution unit. The corrective plan for the Canal Neyba describes the institute's standing practice: "se procede a las firmas de los permisos y los trabajos se inician sin haber pagado las compensaciones correspondientes" — permits are signed and the works begin without the compensation having been paid. The plan also says the execution unit lacked a thorough knowledge of the Bank's OP 4.12.

companies.name: Hanson – Rodríguez, S.R.L.
companies.role: The firm contracted to supervise the Canal Neyba works. Its survey brigade measured the plots to be expropriated and identified the owners, and passed the figures to the project execution unit (corrective resettlement plans, 11 March 2016).

community:
Four corrective resettlement plans published on 11 March 2016 record what happened to farmers on two irrigation works in the Dominican Republic, and say they were written so that the project would be back in compliance with the World Bank's resettlement policy.

On the Canal Lateral Neyba, between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, a new canal was built alongside the old one and a strip of farmland was taken from private plots. The plan for the next stretch of the canal says the expropriations on this stretch happened before the owners were paid: "Dichas expropiaciones ocurrieron, antes de otorgarles las indemnizaciones correspondientes a todos los propietarios de predios, localizados dentro del tramo del Canal Neyba Km 0.00 hasta Km 5.00." Thirteen plots are listed for the first five kilometres, all held without title. Every one carries 2 February 2014 as the date of expropriation. The first group of seven owners was owed 1,343,870 Dominican pesos; half was paid on 14 May 2014 and the rest on 17 July 2014, the plan saying the institution did not have enough money for a single payment. The second group of six owners was paid on 15 October 2014, eight months after the land was taken. The plots run from 0.15 to 24.31 tareas. The plan says no owner lost a whole plot, that nobody was displaced from the place, that no owner lost their means of support and that each lost only part of their fruit trees. It also says that before the land was taken the amounts had been negotiated and agreements signed with every owner authorising INDRHI to expropriate.

On the next stretch of the same canal, from kilometre 5.00 to kilometre 8.50, the plan says the owners were paid before their plots and crops were occupied, following the recommendations of a World Bank social safeguards mission. Its table lists thirteen cases paid on 9 April 2015 and expropriated on 4 May 2015.

On the La Gina system at Miches, in El Seibo, a strip of land was taken to make an access road for the heavy machinery working on the Arroyo Rico dike, and the crops standing on it were taken permanently. The plan says this happened before the owners were paid, and that the land itself was never paid for: "No se pagaron los Predios ocupados provisionalmente, en razón de que serán devueltos, una vez finalizado el Proyecto" — the plots taken provisionally were not paid for, because they are to be returned when the project ends. Only the fruit trees were compensated. Five cases are listed, all held without title, four expropriated on 10 September 2013 and paid on 28 October 2013, the fifth paid on 10 February 2015.

The same plan records two individual losses. Corrective action was taken for one affected person only, Isidro Peralta Amparo, after 63 cocoa trees were cleared on his land; he could not be reached for months because he lives outside the Dominican Republic, and was consulted and compensated once found. On the Río Jayán front, 63 cocoa trees were cleared to cut a bypass channel and the owner was paid on 16 March 2015. Another owner told the Bank's commission that he and the contractor had counted and agreed 75 cocoa trees, "pero sin embargo al final del proceso se cortaron ciento cincuenta (150) arboles Cacaotales" — in the end 150 cocoa trees were cut. The plan adds that apart from that occasion no further complaints were heard.

On the Yuna-Cañabón system at Bonao, six plots were taken permanently, all held without title, for a new intake and feeder canal. Three were paid on 26 December 2014 and expropriated on 8 January 2015; three were paid on 10 April 2015 and expropriated on 5 May 2015. One plot, held by two brothers, was outstanding and was settled on 28 December 2014.
outcome: The completion report of 22 April 2017 says remedial action plans were prepared for the sites concerned with important delays, that a Bank social specialist concluded everyone expropriated had been properly compensated, and that by closing the project was in compliance with the resettlement policy. The La Gina plan says the land taken provisionally there was not paid for because it is to be returned at the end of the project; no document found records the return. The plan says INDRHI has nothing left to pay on that lot. The project closed on 31 October 2016, having been due to close on 31 December 2012.

title: Properties Taken in Manta Before Any Agreement With Their Owners
place: Vía Barbasquillo and the water and sanitation works of Manta, Manabí, Ecuador

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-82890 (8289-EC) for the Manta Public Services Improvement Project (P143996). US$100,000,000, revised to US$99,999,116 and that amount disbursed; the borrower's US$15,600,000 counterpart was revised to zero and none was provided. Borrower the Municipality of Manta with the guarantee of the Republic of Ecuador. Approved 8 August 2013, effective 18 July 2014, mid-term review 11 July 2016, original closing 30 June 2018, actual closing 31 December 2020, after six restructurings. Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12) was triggered because the water and sanitation works needed permanent and temporary land acquisition. The second-order restructuring of March 2019 required the Regional Vice President's approval, to allow loan proceeds to be spent on land acquisition to compensate sixteen landowners affected by the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo; the restructuring of June 2020 reallocated funds between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition". The completion report, dated 30 November 2021, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, monitoring and evaluation Modest, and social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022845 gave the same ratings and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Descentralizado Municipal del Cantón Manta
companies.role: The municipality that borrowed and implemented, through a project implementation unit that had one social specialist and, the completion report says, low capacity. The report records that the unit's legal team, which prepared the resolutions and carried out the land acquisition, feared future problems with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's resettlement policy instead of national law, so it "tended to delay decision making, did not implement agreements, and avoided compliance with OP 4.12". It had never run a project financed by a multilateral bank. The municipality had three different mayors and the unit four different leaders over the project's life, and the report records difficulties caused by political actors who wanted to manipulate the project's procurement (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

companies.name: Empresa Pública Aguas de Manta (EPAM)
companies.role: The municipal water and sanitation company that operates the systems the project built and extended. The completion report quotes its general manager on the effect of the loan on service quality and reports that the project updated and brought into operation the company's commercial system (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

community:
The project rebuilt water, sewerage and street infrastructure in Manta, on the coast of Manabí, which was hit by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake in April 2016.

The Bank's resettlement policy was triggered because the works needed land, permanently and temporarily. The implementation unit prepared a resettlement policy framework in 2016 to deal with people losing access to land, assets or income. The completion report states what happened next: "The PIU's low capacity as well as a high-level of political involvement in the Project contributed to issues with the initial land acquisition processes. Several properties were taken without having all the required permits or without having reached agreements with the owners. This situation occurred for almost a year at the beginning of the Project; the Bank presented its non-conformities in different documents, and the Borrower satisfactorily complied with the required processes."

In March 2019 the Bank restructured the loan, with the approval of its Regional Vice President, so that loan money could be used to compensate sixteen landowners whose land was taken for the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo. In June 2020, six months before the loan closed, a further restructuring moved money between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition".

The completion report's lessons set out why the compensation went wrong. Ecuadorian regulation "does not reach the full replacement cost required by OP 4.12 for land acquisition". The implementation unit was reluctant to go against national rules even though the Bank's rules take precedence in this kind of project, and its legal team was afraid of trouble with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's policy, so it delayed decisions, did not implement agreements and avoided complying with the policy. The Bank "had to escalate this issue to the highest level of management to bring about change and ensure compliance", and an agreement signed with the Comptroller proved useful in getting compliance.

The report says the project finished in compliance with all the requirements of the Bank's Environmental and Social Framework despite these difficulties. The project's rehabilitation works benefited 15,740 household sewerage connections, beating the restructured target of 15,500 by 2 per cent and missing the original target of 17,318 by 9 per cent.
outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020, two and a half years after the original date, with almost all of the US$100 million disbursed. Compensation payments for land acquisition were still being completed six months before closing, and the completion report says the project finished in compliance with the Bank's social requirements, with a social safeguard rating of Moderately Satisfactory. The report's own lesson is that projects in countries whose national rules fall short of replacement cost should carry a separate budget line for land acquisition and resettlement from the start. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

title: Assets destroyed and left uncompensated on the Gabon fibre route at Lalara
place: Lalara, on the fibre optic route from Booué to Oyem, Gabon

lenders.name: World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development)
lenders.role: Project P122776, fourth phase of the Central African Backbone Program, Gabon (CAB4). IBRD Loan 81500, US$58 million, of which US$55,739,093 was disbursed, and IBRD Loan 86290, EUR 20.2 million or about US$23 million equivalent, of which US$23,195,506 was disbursed. Approved 28 March 2012, effective 6 March 2013, mid-term review 30 January 2015, original closing 31 December 2016, actual closing 31 October 2020 (completion report ICR00005105, 9 April 2021). The completion report's financing table shows the US$51 million of government counterpart financing recorded at appraisal revised to nil, with nothing disbursed; the Evaluation Group's review says that, on information the project team gave it, the government's actual contribution was US$53.1 million, of which US$51 million on the original project. Neither document reconciles the two. Five safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The completion report rates the overall outcome Satisfactory, and says the safeguards rating was lowered to Moderately Satisfactory in the final status report. The Evaluation Group's review, dated 21 June 2021 in the Bank's archive record, records the same safeguards finding.

companies.name: Commission Nationale des Travaux d'Intérêt Public pour la Promotion de l'Entrepreneuriat et de l'Emploi (CN-TIPPEE)
companies.role: The public works commission that was the project's implementing unit, responsible for the works, the grievance mechanism and the resettlement and indigenous peoples plans.

community: The loans paid for fibre optic links including Booué to Koumameyong, Lalara, Mitzic, Oyem, Bitam and the Cameroon border. The completion report says the project's overall safeguards rating was lowered to Moderately Satisfactory in the final status report for three reasons: delays in the safeguards audit; "social risks associated with non-compensation for the accidental destruction of assets during fieldwork in Lalara"; and incomplete implementation of the Indigenous Peoples Plan in the field. A footnote adds that the construction operators were asked to compensate those destructions but had not done so by the closing date, "raising the prospects of complaints from people whose assets were destroyed". A second footnote says some indigenous peoples activities were still not carried out. The grievance mechanism was working at the closing date and followed the two environmental and social management plans, but its last revision did not cover gender-based violence. 168 complaints were received, 41 per cent of them about loss of revenue and stalls, and 129 had been resolved by the date of a unit report of 11 March 2021. The government's own account, printed in the completion report, says counterpart funds of around FCFA 3 billion made it possible to compensate project-affected persons, repair non-conformities and finish the works, and that local communities helped resolve complaints during resettlement operations and provided land for the technical centres. No document counts the people whose assets were destroyed at Lalara.
outcome: The project closed on 31 October 2020 with the Lalara destructions uncompensated and the Indigenous Peoples Plan unfinished, and with 129 of the 168 complaints recorded as resolved in a project unit report of 11 March 2021 and the rest still being processed. The Evaluation Group's review says both the Lalara compensation and the indigenous peoples issue were still unresolved when it was written, attributing that to the project team rather than to a document.

title: Compensation paid two years late at Dartlo, and grievances left two years at Telavi
place: Dartlo village, Tusheti, Akhmeta municipality, Kakheti, Georgia

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Regional Development Project, P126033, loan IBRD-81480. Approved 20 March 2012, closed 31 December 2017. US$60 million committed, US$57.27 million disbursed, of a total project cost of US$72.18 million. The completion report of 18 June 2018 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 September 2018 also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Municipal Development Fund of Georgia (MDF)
companies.role: The state fund that finances and manages municipal investment works and was the project's implementing agency, with the Ministry of Finance as borrower. It prepared and implemented the abbreviated resettlement plans and ran the grievance mechanism; its safeguards staff grew from 5 to 12 during the project.

companies.name: National Agency for Cultural Heritage Preservation of Georgia
companies.role: The state heritage agency, which cleared designs and developed the second phase sub-project for Dartlo, a protected heritage village (completion report, 18 June 2018).

community: Three sub-projects moved people or interrupted their livelihoods: Dartlo, a protected village high in Tusheti, and the towns of Telavi and Kvareli. The completion report of 18 June 2018 says the Kvareli plan covered temporary income losses of 33 people, the Telavi plan covered temporary relocation and business interruption for 91 households and 84 businesses, and the Dartlo plan covered 44 residential buildings whose owners had to move out for the duration of the works. The same paragraph says both the Kvareli and the Telavi plans "were fully implemented prior to the start of physical works". The resettlement plan update for Dartlo, dated July 2016, records what happened in the first season. Rehabilitation works started on 33 buildings in 2012. All 33 fell in the category whose residents had to move out for the works, but the update records that seven of them were ruins and that seven more had only small-scale works which the building and supervisory company said needed no temporary relocation, leaving the owners of 19 buildings entitled to compensation under the 2012 plan. "In 2012, no one owner of the buildings has received the compensations." Compensation due for 2012 to 21 affected persons was paid in 2014 to 19 of them, and two were still waiting, with payment planned for 2016 once the plan was updated. The same update counts the entitled owners as 19 in one passage and the persons due payment as 21 in another. The update also records that in 2012 none of the buildings was officially registered and owners were identified from villagers' verbal statements, which later changed who was entitled: one building recorded as having a single owner turned out to have three. At Telavi, the completion report says 37 grievances submitted in 2014 were not addressed until 2016. A footnote says those grievances "involved claims by affected business owners that the provided compensation did not fully cover losses incurred as a result of the Project". An independent consultant was appointed in the summer of 2014 to help settle them and to check whether compensation had been paid in line with Bank policy; the report says the assessment helped address the complaints and "confirmed compliance". Separately, the report records that for an extended period environmental supervision and reporting were poor, "creating substantial risks for the livelihood of affected communities, health of workers": construction companies operated without adequate arrangements for waste disposal, and there were "obvious deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety as well as in managing disturbance of communities residing in and around work sites". The completion report says the project was compliant with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that the Dartlo plan was completed without grievances or complaints.
outcome: The works are finished and the project closed at the end of 2017. By the July 2016 plan update, two of the Dartlo owners due compensation for 2012 had still not been paid, four years after the works on their houses. The Telavi grievances were settled in 2016 and the lender's assessment found compensation had complied with its policy. No independent account of the Dartlo or Telavi compensation was found.

title: A road worker killed and a resident's house damaged on the Igoeti highway works
place: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, Shida Kartli, Georgia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second East-West Highway Improvement Project, P094044, credits IDA-43730 and IDA-45120. Approved 18 December 2007, closed 30 June 2012. XDR 34.72 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 October 2013.

companies.name: Roads Department of Georgia
companies.role: The national road agency, moved in the 2009 ministerial reforms from the Ministry of Economic Development to the new Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure, and the project's implementing agency. Its Resettlement Unit, four staff plus a hired consultant, handled land acquisition and compensation. The completion report does not name the construction contractors, calling them "the first road contractor" and the contractor hired in June 2011.

community: One of the first road contractor's local employees was killed while performing a pavement test on the project section. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", and that the contractor "refused to pay compensation to the victim's family for about 1.5 years, despite constant reminders by the Bank Team" and the Roads Department. The report's lessons section says the accident shows that traffic safety during road construction works remains a problem, and that payment to a contractor should be refused where it has not met safety requirements. The same contractor started civil works before land acquisition from a resident of Igoeti village was officially completed, and in doing so damaged her house and made improper use of her land. That case stayed open from 2009 until 25 June 2012, when she signed an agreement accepting GEL 11,139, about US$6,700, for 954 square metres of land and 62 fruit trees; payment took effect on 9 July 2012. She had already been paid GEL 45,000, about US$27,270, in February 2011 for damage to her summer house during construction. The report says the first contractor's work was unsatisfactory in many instances, that it knew of design errors and "took advantage of the situation", and that it failed to comply with the environmental management plan, especially on storage and disposal of materials. Land take ran well beyond the original plan: the original resettlement plan envisioned 167 land plots covering 91,968 square metres on the Igoeti to Sveneti section, and the number of plots actually affected within the right of way of the main alignment reached 192, covering 146,914 square metres. The completion report attributes the difference to inconsistent right-of-way data and poor coordination between the cadastral data in the plan and the data used in the preliminary design. About 4 more hectares of private land were needed for connecting roads to neighbouring villages. The completion report says all compensation was paid by the end of the project, totalling GEL 1,343,773, about US$0.81 million, and that all outstanding cases were resolved to the satisfaction of the affected people.
outcome: The highway section is built. The first contractor's contract was allowed to expire and another contractor was hired in June 2011 to finish the works and repair the defective ones. The family of the dead worker was paid after about a year and a half, according to the completion report, which does not give the amount. The Igoeti land case closed with payment in July 2012.

title: Six farmers lose the land they worked to the Kumasi lands office site

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P120636, Second Land Administration Project. IDA Credit 48700, US$50 million, of which US$46,795,104 was disbursed; Trust Fund TF-14256, US$2,879,706, of which US$2,500,919 was disbursed; and IDA 63450, US$35 million, of which nothing was disbursed. Approved 31 March 2011, effective 8 August 2011, mid-term review 2 June 2014, original closing 31 March 2016, actual closing 20 January 2020 (completion report ICR00005225, 18 June 2020, which revises an earlier completion report of 19 October 2018). The US$5 million of government counterpart funding was not provided in full: less than US$1 million was disbursed. Environmental category B, partial assessment. Two safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The revised completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, where the earlier completion report of 19 October 2018 rated it Moderately Satisfactory; it gives the reason as the failure of the project and the Lands Commission to address the bottlenecks in deeds and title registration and to meet the outcome indicators, which leaves efficacy Modest. The Evaluation Group reviewed both reports: its review of 22 March 2019 and its review dated 31 December 2020 in the Bank's archive record each rate the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Lands Commission, Ghana
companies.role: The state body that manages public land and keeps the land register, under the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources. The regional head office built at Kumasi under the project was its office.

companies.name: Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, Ghana
companies.role: The ministry that held the project coordination unit and, with the Lands Commission, implemented the project.

community: The project built a regional head office for the land sector agencies at Kumasi, on undeveloped government land. The revised completion report says the environmental and social assessment prepared for that land covered a site "which caused economic displacement of six (6) farmers", and that although the project did not physically displace anyone it economically displaced six farmers, so an Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan was prepared. The six is the resettlement plan's own count. The abbreviated plan surveyed the Kumasi site on 11 and 12 October 2010 and found six farmers there, one woman and five men aged between 28 and 65, two of them keeping pigs and the rest growing cassava, plantain and maize, earning between GH¢10 and GH¢400 a month; it records that they knew they would have to move their activities before the civil works began and that they wanted cash compensation for the loss of their farms. The appraisal document of March 2011 carried the same figure, and noted that people occupying the land earmarked for the office could lose their livelihood. The revised completion report of 2020 is the document that attaches a completed harm to the figure, saying the site "caused economic displacement of six (6) farmers" and that the project "involved economic displacement of six farmers". The report says the resettlement activities on economic displacement and livelihood restoration were carried out with proper disclosure of information and the involvement of stakeholders and that no issues arose, and that based on reports and evidence from the field the resettlement was in compliance with the lender's policies. The plan put the whole resettlement budget at GH¢9,432.70. No outcome document says what the six farmers were paid. The first completion report, of 19 October 2018, does not mention the six farmers at all: it says only that the two safeguard policies were triggered and that no issues arose during implementation. The construction at Kumasi was delayed, and the completion report names those delays, with the land information system contract, as the clear exceptions to otherwise adequate project management.
outcome: The project closed on 20 January 2020. The completion report records the resettlement as complete and the safeguards rating as Satisfactory at the time the project's main activities finished in January 2019.

title: Compensation paid to six of the fifteen on the Bijilo cable route in The Gambia
place: Cable route from Bijilo Beach to the Sukuta institutional area along the Kombo Beach Highway, Bijilo, West Coast Region, The Gambia

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P122402, West Africa Regional Communications Infrastructure Project, second project under the first phase (WARCIP APL 1B). IDA Grant H7130 to The Gambia, US$35 million, of which US$32,563,720 was disbursed; IDA Grant H7120 to Burkina Faso, US$23 million, of which US$19,948,274 was disbursed; IDA Grant H7140 to Guinea, US$34 million, of which US$31,755,664 was disbursed; and IDA Credit 62220 to Burkina Faso, US$20 million, of which US$16,651,819 was disbursed. Approved 21 June 2011, effective 31 October 2011, mid-term review 2 June 2014, original closing 31 December 2016, actual closing 30 July 2021 (completion report ICR00005569, 25 February 2022). Environmental category B. Four safeguard policies were triggered, which the completion report names as Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.36), Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and the Evaluation Group's review, dated 23 August 2022 in the Bank's archive record, agrees.

companies.name: Ministry of Information and Communication Infrastructure (MOICI), The Gambia
companies.role: The ministry made responsible by the resettlement plan for carrying it out, through the state telecommunications company. The completion report names the dispute between the two over who should release the funds as the main cause of the delay.

companies.name: Gambia Telecommunications Company Limited (GAMTEL)
companies.role: The state telecommunications company through which the ministry was to implement the resettlement plan.

companies.name: SAL Consult Limited
companies.role: The Accra consultancy that wrote The Gambia resettlement plan of May 2011, which counted the people the cable route would affect.

community: The cable route in The Gambia runs from Bijilo Beach to the Sukuta institutional area along the Kombo Beach Highway, past houses, shops, workshops, petrol stations, empty plots and a hotel. The resettlement plan of May 2011 listed 27 structures or plots and said 27 people would be affected, with no permanent or temporary structure lost and no land acquisition needed; it described the effects as temporary inconvenience. The completion report says that in June 2013, two years after the plan was written, implementation had not started, and that the number of people affected was then listed as 15, entitled to about US$1,500 in all. That 15 is also the plan's figure, and in the plan it is not a count of people: the plan says it "covered 15 shops and 4 residential houses which will be impacted by the project", and its Annex 1 lists 15 entitlement entries by initials or trading name — among them a petrol station, an inn, a lumber shop, a charcoal and firewood seller and two concrete-products sites — with a disturbance allowance and assistance for each and a total of 37,923.49 dalasi. The completion report gives the same 15 as a count of people affected. A year later the payments were still not finished. Radio announcements in local languages and repeated visits followed, and "Compensation was provided to the six people who were located." A footnote cites a monitoring report of 7 October 2014 from the ministry and a supervision mission report of January 2015 acknowledging payment to just six of the 15. The report says many of the others had moved away and that different businesses were on the sites. The report also finds no documentation that the contractor applied the environmental management plan, and none that the environmental and social measures for the operating phase were adopted. In Burkina Faso, the works from Ouagadougou to Paga partly affected structures and caused temporary loss of revenue: 277 households were identified as affected and 274 received money, FCFA 23 million or about US$40,000, and the report adds that the resettlement completion report said all compensation measures had been carried out. On the Dindéogo to Zabré extension, 198 households were affected and all 198 were paid, FCFA 19 million or about US$33,000. The works between Fada and Pama were not built, for security reasons.
outcome: The project closed on 30 July 2021 with compensation paid to six of the 15 entries on The Gambia plan's compensation annex and not to the rest. The Evaluation Group's review repeats the six of 15 and adds that, according to the project team, only six could be identified after an extensive campaign and that the actions taken were appropriate and sufficient; that is a statement by staff and not a document.

title: Three Households Resettled and Land Taken in Two Hundred and One Cases on Honduras’s Second Road Credit
place: The San Lorenzo–Olanchito, El Porvenir–Marale and La Esperanza–Camasca roads and the El Porvenir by-pass, Honduras

lenders.name: International Development Association (World Bank)
lenders.role: Second Road Rehabilitation and Improvement Project, filed as Honduras Road Rehabilitation and Improvement II (P109058), Credit 4466-HN, 29,600,000 Special Drawing Rights, financing agreement with the Republic of Honduras dated 13 October 2008, with an additional financing, Credit 4583-HN, of 16,800,000 Special Drawing Rights dated 2 August 2010. The completion report of 25 November 2015 says in its social safeguards paragraph that "The Project triggered the Bank safeguard policies OP 4.12 for Involuntary Resettlement and OP 4.10 for Indigenous Peoples", that an abbreviated involuntary resettlement plan and an indigenous peoples plan were prepared and disclosed, and that resettlement action plans were prepared and implemented for each road corridor to which they applied. It says that "During implementation, only minor issues were encountered such as administrative delays in the payment of compensation to affected parties." It rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory. No evaluation review of this report was harvested.

lenders.name: Central American Bank for Economic Integration (BCIE)
lenders.role: Co-financier of the road works. The completion report of 25 November 2015 gives the project an estimated total cost of 64.6 million dollars, of which 48.6 million from IDA Credit 4466 "together with co-financing of US$15 million from the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (BCIE) and GOH financing of $1 million", and puts 14 million of the BCIE money into Component 1, the rehabilitation and improvement of the roads on which the land was taken, and 1 million into implementation support. A footnote to the report’s financing annex says BCIE "increased credit amount to US$22 mn based on revised estimated costs of La Esperanza – Camasca construction". The report does not say which credit paid for the works on any one corridor.

companies.name: Secretaría de Infraestructura y Servicios Públicos (INSEP)
companies.role: The Honduran public works ministry that ran the project and managed the right of way; the completion report also calls it SOPTRAVI, the name of the ministry when the project began. The report says social management capacity inside it went from effectively none at the start of the project to three full-time specialists at completion, and that the main focus was managing the right of way and building a more proactive capacity on land acquisition and resettlement.

community:
The completion report of 25 November 2015 counts the land taken for the road works. Its sentence runs: the preparation and execution of resettlement plans for all the road improvements "was effectively carried, with the total number of cases identified and resolved with compensation effected in full as follows: San Lorenzo – Olanchito 8 cases; El Porvenir – Marale 25 cases (plus 59 cases related to the acquisition of land for the construction of the El Porvenir by-pass); La Esperanza - Camasca 109 cases (some additions possible given the works have not yet been completed). In 3 cases, households were resettled in all other cases compensation was paid in an aggregate total amount of US$0.45 million."

So three households were moved and the rest of the 201 cases were settled with money, 450,000 dollars between them. The report says compensation was effected in full, and that more cases on the La Esperanza to Camasca road were possible because the works were not finished when the report was written.

On how the payments were made, the report's safeguards section says that during implementation "only minor issues were encountered such as administrative delays in the payment of compensation to affected parties". It gives no count of the people affected by those delays and no length for them.
outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2015, having been due to close on 30 June 2013. The completion report says all 201 cases were identified and resolved with compensation effected in full, and that the works on the La Esperanza to Camasca road were not yet complete, so more cases were possible. No document found reports on the three resettled households after the move, or on how long the payment delays lasted.
